originalGroup.material:
An umbrella and two names

Last Friday, we ____1____ (find) an umbrella in front of the school hall. It was lying ____2____ front of a bench, with nobody nearby. Two ____3____ (name) had been written on its label, one above the other.

Our teacher asked whether we knew anyone ____4____ name matched either one. I recognised the lower name, but that student had left our class the previous year. I agreed ____5____ (take) the umbrella to the office rather than leave it outside.

The umbrella ____6____ (keep) there until the owner could be found. An office assistant looked ____7____ (careful) at the label. She noticed that the upper name was written in newer ink. It was different ____8____ the name in the old class list I had remembered.

Later, a younger student came to ask about the umbrella. She explained that it had belonged to her brother, who was three years ____9____ (old) than she was, before he passed it to her. The two names were not a mistake; they recorded two owners.

Before returning it, the assistant asked a few questions about its colour and handle. The student's answers matched, so she handed it over. I had learned that old records could help, but I needed to compare ____10____ (they) with what was in front of me.

originalGroup.material:
A changing sky

Our class ____1____ (plan) a short weather record last month. One morning brought such ____2____ unusual mixture of sunshine and showers that we decided to begin immediately. Several ____3____ (window) in our room looked towards the playground, giving us a clear view without going outside.

We used a photograph ____4____ (take) by the teacher as the first entry. It showed wet ground under bright sunlight. Our record would include short descriptions as well ____5____ pictures, because one image could not show how quickly the sky had changed.

Instead of ____6____ (write) only 'good' or 'bad', we described what we could observe. A student ____7____ coat was still damp explained that it had rained heavily on her walk to school, even though the sun was shining now.

We worked more ____8____ (careful) after noticing how easily a general label could hide differences. The final record ____9____ (check) by two classmates before it went on the wall. They corrected one time and moved a photograph beside the matching description.

The project did not make ____10____ (we) weather experts. It helped us distinguish a brief observation from a description of the whole day, and to say when we had actually looked.

The names in the programme

After ____1____ (choose) a programme design, our drama group sent it for printing. The first copies ____2____ (print) on Thursday, one day before the show. Their large letters were easier to read ____3____ those in the earlier version.

However, one actor's name had been ____4____ (mistake) written with the wrong final letter. The girl ____5____ was playing the narrator noticed it while checking her lines. She did not want a public argument; she simply asked whether we could correct the remaining copies.

We agreed ____6____ (check) the whole cast list rather than change only that one name. Two ____7____ (name) had similar spellings, which explained how the error had happened. ____8____ spite of the limited time, we made a corrected version and checked it with the actors before printing again.

One earlier copy ____9____ (keep) with a note explaining the change. We did not want it to be mistaken for the final programme later. Everyone was ____10____ (busy) than expected that afternoon, but the extra care mattered.

At the show, the narrator thanked us quietly. The correction was small on the page, yet important to the person it named. I learned that checking names was part of respecting the work behind a performance, not merely a final decoration.

A family recipe notebook

The oldest page in our family recipe notebook had been ____1____ (write) by my grandmother. Several ____2____ (memory) were attached to it: a birthday meal, a winter visit and a story about a cake that did not rise.

When we decided to make a new copy, I was responsible ____3____ preparing the pages. Before ____4____ (serve) dinner one evening, I asked each person to explain a favourite recipe. My aunt, ____5____ handwriting I could recognise immediately, showed me where she had changed one of Grandma's instructions.

I noticed that two people sometimes described the same dish ____6____ (different). One began with quantities; another began with how the food should look. We decided ____7____ (record) both accounts, clearly naming their owners rather than pretending there was only one family version.

The notebook now contains short stories as well ____8____ recipes. What ____9____ (surprise) me most was how often a small detail brought back a whole occasion. A mark beside one ingredient could lead to a conversation about somebody who had cooked it years earlier.

We kept the original pages and stored ____10____ (they) separately from the new copy. The new book was easier to read, but the old handwriting remained part of the family's record. Making a clear copy did not require removing the signs of how the recipes had travelled between people.
